title: Gradient Descent
description: Gradient Descent is the 2019 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of synthwave metal about how machines learn. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Qword plays neon shred guitar, Wyrd goes back to analog synths from the 1980s, and Bytes plays big gated-reverb drums over drum machines and sings backup. The Turing test, search and A*, minimax, expert systems, Bayes, training data, neural networks, gradient descent, overfitting, clustering, reinforcement learning and generative models. Written after the label trained an AI on every song the band ever recorded and released it as Procedural Bots. It topped the charts for a week, until fans noticed every song had a duck with five legs. Play loud. Count the legs.
tagline: The 2019 synthwave metal album from Procedural Byts: an artificial intelligence course in twelve songs, and the AI band with the five-legged duck.
lineup: The four-piece, against its own imitation. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays shred lead guitar. Wyrd plays retro analog synthesizers. Bytes plays gated-reverb drums and drum machines and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and the first person to count the duck’s legs. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits, back to full shred for synthwave, and the only member Procedural Bots could imitate convincingly. Qword took it as a compliment, for about an hour.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, back on the analog synths of 1985, and the builder of the spam filter that hid every letter about the duck.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, big gated-reverb drums over drum machines, and backing vocals. His practice tapes are why the AI band was always a beat early.

members.name: Null
members.bio: The one member the model could never imitate. Its duck kept quacking. The real one doesn’t.

story.heading: Procedural Bots
paragraphs: In 2019, without asking, the band’s label fed every song Procedural Byts had ever recorded into a neural network and released the result as an album by a new band: Procedural Bots. It went straight to the top of the charts.

It lasted a week. Then fans noticed that every Procedural Bots song had a duck in it, and every duck had five legs. The model had learned that Procedural Byts songs always have a duck. It had never learned how many legs a duck has.

There were other tells. The training data included Bytes’s practice tapes, so the AI band always came in a beat early. And because it had only ever heard this band, it believed every song in the world was about computer science.

The one member it could never imitate was Null. The AI kept generating a duck that quacked. Fans who had listened since 1989 knew the duck had quacked exactly once, and that’s how they could always tell.

So the band made an album about how machines actually learn, to understand what had happened to them. Synthwave was the obvious sound for a story about machines from the future built out of the past: Wyrd went back to analog synthesizers from the 1980s, Bytes got his gated-reverb drums back, and Qword’s solos turned neon.

At the release show, the band played fans a blind test, one song by Procedural Byts and one by Procedural Bots. Most picked correctly. Several picked the wrong one on purpose, because the five-legged duck was funnier.

cover_sub: The 2019 album. A label trained a machine to be the band. It got the duck wrong.

songs.title: The Turing Test

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: In nineteen fifty Turing asked if a machine could think,
Then said, let’s play a game instead, and see if they’re in sync.
A judge, a person and a machine, all typing through the night,
If the judge can’t tell which one is which, maybe the machine is right!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: The Turing test! (Who is who?)
The Turing test! (Is it you?)
Fooling the judge is not the same as knowing what you say,
The Turing test, the Turing test, the imitation game we play!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Some chatbots fooled the judges with a joke and with a dodge,
Pretending to be someone young, a clever camouflage.
But passing for a person doesn’t mean there’s understanding,
Intelligence is harder than a mask that’s just pretending!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Human? (Or machine?) Machine? (Or human?)
Can you tell? (Can you tell?) Does it matter? (Does it matter?)

parts.label: Imitation game: Qword and Wyrd
parts.desc: Qword and Wyrd trade phrases, and Wyrd’s synth is programmed to sound exactly like a guitar. By the third exchange, nobody in the room can tell which phrase came from which instrument.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: The Turing test! (Who is who?)
The Turing test! (Is it you?)
Fooling the judge is not the same as knowing what you say,
The Turing test, the Turing test, the imitation game we play!

songs.note: Alan Turing called it the imitation game. The band played it with fans in 2019, using one of its own songs and one by Procedural Bots.
songs.lesson: In 1950, Alan Turing proposed the imitation game: a judge has a text conversation with a person and a machine, and if the judge can’t reliably tell which is which, the machine passes. Critics point out that passing, sometimes with tricks like a 2014 chatbot pretending to be a teenager, doesn’t prove understanding; John Searle’s Chinese Room argument makes the same point. The test is still a useful way into the question of what “intelligence” means.

songs.title: A Star

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A maze of rooms and roads, and somewhere there’s a goal,
Search it breadth by breadth, or dive deep into the hole.
But a heuristic is a hunch of how far there’s left to go,
And A star adds the cost so far to what it thinks it knows!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: A star! (Cost so far!)
A star! (Plus the guess!)
F equals G plus H, and it finds the shortest way,
A star, A star, the best route home today!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: If the guess is never longer than the truth, the answer will be best,
An admissible heuristic, and it beats out all the rest.
Straight-line distance on a map is never longer than the road,
So A star finds the shortest path and doesn’t carry extra load!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Breadth first! (Every way!) Depth first! (Too deep!)
Greedy! (Too fast!) A star! (Just right, and cheap!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword tries a few directions on the neck, guessing which is closest to the target note, then commits to the one with the lowest total cost and lands on the target in the fewest moves.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: A star! (Cost so far!)
A star! (Plus the guess!)
F equals G plus H, and it finds the shortest way,
A star, A star, the best route home today!

songs.note: The 2019 tour bus finally had a navigation system. Bytes named it after the algorithm inside it.
songs.lesson: A lot of AI is search: states, actions and a goal. Uninformed searches like breadth-first and depth-first explore blindly. Informed search uses a heuristic, an estimate of how far is left to go. A* expands the option with the lowest f = g + h, the cost so far plus the estimated cost remaining, and as long as the heuristic never overestimates (straight-line distance on a map, for example), it’s guaranteed to find the shortest path.

songs.title: Minimax

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I make my move to win, and you make yours to make me lose,
Look ahead a few moves deep and see which path to choose.
Assume the other side is smart and plays the best they can,
Maximize my worst case, that’s the minimax plan!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Minimax! (Your move!)
Minimax! (My move!)
I take the max, you take the min, and down the tree we go,
Minimax, minimax, and checkmate, there you go!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The game tree grows too fast to see it all the way down,
So prune the branches that don’t matter, alpha-beta all around.
In ninety-seven Deep Blue played the champion and won,
Two hundred million moves a second, and the game was done!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Max! (My turn!) Min! (Your turn!)
Prune! (Don’t look!) Win! (Learn!)

parts.label: Chess match: Qword and Wyrd
parts.desc: Qword and Wyrd play the solo as a game: each phrase is a move, and each answer is the one that makes the other’s next move hardest. Wyrd looks two moves ahead. Qword looks three. Qword wins.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Minimax! (Your move!)
Minimax! (My move!)
I take the max, you take the min, and down the tree we go,
Minimax, minimax, and checkmate, there you go!

songs.note: In 1997, a computer beat the world chess champion. In 2019, the band played chess against the tour bus navigation system. It lost, but only because Bytes moved its pieces.
songs.lesson: For two-player games, minimax search assumes the opponent always plays their best: you choose the move whose worst possible outcome is the best. Game trees grow explosively, so alpha-beta pruning skips branches that can’t change the result, and searches stop at a set depth and score positions with an evaluation function. IBM’s Deep Blue beat world champion Garry Kasparov in 1997.

songs.title: Expert System

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: If the fever’s high and the rash is red, then check for this disease,
A thousand rules from human experts written down with ease.
The inference engine chains them up and reaches a conclusion,
Knowledge in a box of rules, the symbolic revolution!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Expert system! (If, then!)
Expert system! (Again!)
Facts and rules and reasoning, and it tells you why it knows,
Expert system, expert system, and the knowledge grows!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: It can explain its answer, every rule it used along the way,
But the world is full of exceptions that the rules can’t say.
Ask it something new and it breaks right at the edge,
The rules are only what we wrote, and the world falls off the ledge!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Forward chaining! (From the facts!)
Backward chaining! (From the goal!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd’s synth line follows strict rules: if the last note went up, go down; if it was long, play two short ones. It sounds perfect, until Bytes plays something the rules never covered, and the synth just stops.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Expert system! (If, then!)
Expert system! (Again!)
Facts and rules and reasoning, and it tells you why it knows,
Expert system, expert system, and the knowledge grows!

songs.note: In the 1980s, the band’s label tried to replace its accountant with a program made of rules. It is still running.
songs.lesson: Symbolic AI represents knowledge explicitly, as logic and rules. Expert systems, popular in the 1970s and 1980s (MYCIN, for diagnosing infections, is a famous one), capture an expert’s if-then rules and use an inference engine to chain them to a conclusion, and they can explain exactly which rules they used. Their weakness is brittleness: they fail on anything outside their rules, and writing all those rules takes enormous effort.

songs.title: Prior

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I thought it was unlikely, and then I saw the sign,
A little bit of evidence, and I changed my mind.
Start with what you believed before, then weigh what you just saw,
Update it with Bayes, and that’s the reasoning law!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Prior! (What I believed!)
Evidence! (What I perceived!)
Posterior! (What I know now!)
Bayes, Bayes, and here’s how!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The word “free” is in the email, is it spam or is it not?
How often is it in the spam, and in the good mail that we got?
Multiply the prior by the likelihood you see,
And the probability updates, and the answer comes to me!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Uncertain! (Not sure!) Probable! (More sure!)
Update! (Again!) A hundred percent? (Never!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble starts the solo unsure, playing a phrase softly. Each time the band answers in agreement, she plays it with more confidence. When Bytes disagrees once, she pulls back a little, then keeps going.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Prior! (What I believed!)
Evidence! (What I perceived!)
Posterior! (What I know now!)
Bayes, Bayes, and here’s how!

songs.note: Wyrd built a spam filter for the band’s fan mail. It sent every letter that mentioned a duck to the spam folder. It took a week to find them.
songs.lesson: AI often has to reason under uncertainty. Bayes’ theorem updates a prior belief with new evidence to get a posterior belief: P(H | E) = P(E | H) × P(H) / P(E). Naive Bayes classifiers, like early spam filters, combine the evidence from many words, assuming each one is independent. Probabilistic reasoning keeps degrees of belief instead of pretending to be certain.

songs.title: Training Data

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Show me a thousand pictures, and you tell me which are cats,
I’ll find the patterns in the pixels, and I’ll learn from all of that.
Supervised, the answers given, labels on each one,
Then show me something new, and I’ll guess before you’re done!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Training data! (What I learn from!)
Training data! (Where I’m born from!)
Garbage in and garbage out, I only know what I was shown,
Training data, training data, and the patterns are your own!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The features are the measurements, the label is the truth,
Classify to pick a category, regress to find a number for proof.
Skew the data and you skew the model, it learns the bias too,
A model is a mirror of the data that you gave it to view!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Labeled! (Supervised!) Features! (Measured!)
Classify! (Which one?) Regress! (How much?)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: The band plays Qword ten short example licks. Qword plays them back, then plays an eleventh that nobody taught, in exactly the same style. That’s learning from examples.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Training data! (What I learn from!)
Training data! (Where I’m born from!)
Garbage in and garbage out, I only know what I was shown,
Training data, training data, and the patterns are your own!

songs.note: The label trained Procedural Bots on every song the band ever recorded, including Bytes’s practice tapes. That’s why the AI band was always a beat early.
songs.lesson: Machine learning finds patterns in data instead of following rules someone wrote. In supervised learning, each training example has features (measurements) and a label (the right answer). Classification predicts a category, like cat or dog; regression predicts a number, like a price. A model is a mirror of its data: if the training data is skewed or biased, the model will be too. Garbage in, garbage out.

songs.title: Neural Net

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A neuron takes its inputs and it weighs them one by one,
Adds them up, applies a function, and decides if it should run.
Stack them into layers and connect them all in rows,
The input to the hidden to the output, and it grows!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Neural net! (Weights and sums!)
Neural net! (Here it comes!)
Layer after layer, and the patterns come alive,
Neural net, neural net, deep enough to thrive!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A single layer draws a line, and it can’t solve XOR,
Add a hidden layer and it learns a whole lot more.
Deep learning stacks them many deep, with data by the ton,
And the graphics cards from oh-four are how the training’s done!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Input! (In!) Hidden! (Within!)
Output! (Out!) Activate! (Shout!)

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd plays one note, which fans out into a layer of four harmonies, then a layer of eight, each weighted differently, until they all combine into a single chord at the end: the output.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Neural net! (Weights and sums!)
Neural net! (Here it comes!)
Layer after layer, and the patterns come alive,
Neural net, neural net, deep enough to thrive!

songs.note: The graphics cards from Rasterize, back in 2004, are the reason this album could exist. Neural networks run on them.
songs.lesson: An artificial neural network is built from simple units, “neurons,” that each take a weighted sum of their inputs and pass it through a nonlinear activation function. They’re arranged in layers: input, hidden and output. A single layer can only separate data with a straight line, so it can’t even learn XOR, but hidden layers make networks far more powerful. Deep learning stacks many layers and trains them on huge datasets using GPUs.

songs.title: Gradient Descent

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I’m standing on a mountain in the dark, and I want the valley floor,
I can’t see the bottom, but I feel the slope, and that’s what I’m looking for.
Take a step downhill, then feel the ground again,
Step by step the error falls, and the model learns, and then…

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Gradient descent! (Step down!)
Gradient descent! (Lower ground!)
Measure the loss, find the slope, and take a step the other way,
Gradient descent, gradient descent, a little better every day!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The learning rate’s the step size, and too big you jump right past,
Too small and you’ll be walking down that mountain till the last.
Backpropagation sends the error back through every weight,
Every weight gets nudged a bit, and the model’s doing great!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Loss! (How wrong?) Gradient! (Which way?)
Step! (Downhill!) Repeat! (All day!)
Local minimum! (Stuck in a dip!) Try again! (Another trip!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword walks the solo down the neck one step at a time, feeling for the lowest note. Once, Qword takes too big a step and overshoots, climbs back, then takes smaller steps until landing on the lowest note on the album.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Gradient descent! (Step down!)
Gradient descent! (Lower ground!)
Measure the loss, find the slope, and take a step the other way,
Gradient descent, gradient descent, a little better every day!

songs.note: The title track. The melody walks downhill one step at a time and lands on the lowest note on the album.
songs.lesson: Training a model means minimizing a loss function that measures how wrong it is. Gradient descent works out the gradient, the slope of the loss for every parameter, and takes a small step in the opposite direction, again and again. The learning rate sets the step size: too big and you overshoot, too small and it takes forever. Backpropagation calculates all those gradients efficiently through the layers of a network. Training can settle in a local minimum, though in very large networks that turns out to matter less than people once feared.

songs.title: Overfit

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I memorized the practice test, each answer, every line,
Then the real exam had different questions, and I couldn’t shine.
A model that remembers every point it ever saw
Learns the noise along with the signal, and that’s the fatal flaw!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Overfit! (Too tight!)
Overfit! (Not right!)
Perfect on the training set and failing on the new,
Overfit, overfit, it never learned what’s true!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Split the data, train on most, and test on what it’s never seen,
Validation tells you if it learned, or if it’s just a memory machine.
Simpler models, much more data, regularize, and stop in time,
Underfit is far too simple, and the middle is the line!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Training accuracy! (A hundred percent!)
Test accuracy! (Where’d it go?)
Generalize! (Generalize!) That’s all we need to know!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword learns one practice riff so exactly that every accidental scrape and buzz gets copied too. Given a new riff, Qword plays it with the old riff’s mistakes in it. Then Qword strips everything back, keeps only the shape, and plays the new riff right.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Overfit! (Too tight!)
Overfit! (Not right!)
Perfect on the training set and failing on the new,
Overfit, overfit, it never learned what’s true!

songs.note: Procedural Bots was trained only on the band’s songs, so it thought all music was about computer science.
songs.lesson: A model overfits when it learns its training data too closely, noise and all: it scores perfectly on the training data and badly on anything new. A model that’s too simple underfits. To check how well a model generalizes, hold back test data it never sees during training, plus validation data for tuning. Remedies include more data, simpler models, regularization and stopping training early.

songs.title: Cluster

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: No labels this time, no answers, nothing named,
Just a pile of points, and the patterns aren’t explained.
Find the ones that look alike and gather them as one,
Unsupervised, and the groups appear when you are done!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Cluster! (Find the groups!)
Cluster! (Birds of a feather!)
No one told it what to look for, but it found them all the same,
Cluster, cluster, and the patterns have no name!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: K-means picks some centers and it sends each point to the nearest,
Moves the centers to the middle and repeats until it’s clearest.
Pick the number of groups yourself, and hope you chose it right,
Then look at what it found and give the groups a name tonight!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Assign! (To the nearest!) Update! (To the middle!)
Repeat! (Until it settles!) And now solve the riddle!

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd scatters notes all over the keyboard at random. Slowly they drift together into three groups, low, middle and high, each pulled toward its own center, until you can hear three clusters clearly.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Cluster! (Find the groups!)
Cluster! (Birds of a feather!)
No one told it what to look for, but it found them all the same,
Cluster, cluster, and the patterns have no name!

songs.note: Wyrd let an algorithm sort the band’s fans by what they bought at the merch table. It found three groups: T-shirt people, poster people and duck people. The duck people were the largest.
songs.lesson: Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no labels. Clustering groups similar items together. The k-means algorithm picks k starting centers, assigns every point to its nearest center, moves each center to the middle of its group, and repeats until nothing changes. You have to choose k yourself, and it’s up to you to work out what the clusters mean.

songs.title: Reward

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Nobody tells me the right answer, I try it and I see,
A reward when I get it right, and nothing comes to me.
Play a million games against myself and learn from every one,
Reinforcement, trial and error, till I’ve learned how it’s done!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Reward! (Do it again!)
Reward! (Learn from the pain!)
Explore to find the new, exploit the best you know,
Reward, reward, and watch the agent grow!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The agent acts in the world, and the world gives back a score,
It learns a policy to choose the moves that earn it more.
In twenty sixteen it played the game of Go and beat the best,
A move no human would have made, and it passed the test!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Explore! (Try something new!) Exploit! (Do what works!)
Reward! (The goal!) Penalty! (It hurts!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes tries a new fill and gets a cheer when part of it works and silence when it doesn’t. Each attempt keeps what earned the cheer and tries something new for the rest. By the eighth try, the fill is perfect.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Reward! (Do it again!)
Reward! (Learn from the pain!)
Explore to find the new, exploit the best you know,
Reward, reward, and watch the agent grow!

songs.note: In 2016, a program taught itself to play Go well enough to beat one of the best players in the world. The band taught Bytes a new drum fill the same way, with snacks.
songs.lesson: In reinforcement learning, an agent learns by acting in an environment and getting rewards or penalties, with the goal of learning a policy that earns the most reward over time. It has to balance exploration, trying something new, against exploitation, doing what already works. DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat top Go player Lee Sedol in 2016 by combining reinforcement learning, neural networks and search.

songs.title: Five Legs

parts.label: Intro (spoken)
lines: The label trained it on every song we ever made.
It learned that our songs have a duck in them.
It never learned how many legs a duck has.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: It learned to write our songs by guessing what comes next,
One word after another, predicting all the text.
It sounded just like us, the riffs, the words, the tone,
But it never knew a duck, it only knew the ones we’d shown.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Five legs! (It’s not a duck!)
Five legs! (Just guessing luck!)
Plausible is not the same as true, and a pattern’s not a mind,
Five legs, five legs, check what it designed!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: It learned our blind spots with our songs, the things we never saw,
And it gave its answers confidently, every confident flaw.
Ask it where it learned it, and ask who gave consent,
A human has to check the work, whatever it has sent!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Can it explain? (Not always!) Was it fair? (Check it!)
Who taught it? (We did!) Who’s responsible? (We are!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays a perfect imitation of the AI band’s guitar: every note plausible, every bend in place, and one wrong note repeated in every phrase, like a fifth leg. Then Qword plays the same solo as a person, slightly imperfect and completely right.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Five legs! (It’s not a duck!)
Five legs! (Just guessing luck!)
Plausible is not the same as true, and a pattern’s not a mind,
Five legs, five legs, check what it designed!

songs.note: Procedural Bots topped the charts for a week. Then fans noticed every song had a duck in it, and every duck had five legs.
songs.lesson: Generative models, like the language models that appeared around 2019 (GPT-2, for example), create text, images or music by predicting what’s likely to come next based on their training data. The output can be fluent and still wrong, which people call hallucination. These models absorb the biases and blind spots of their data, often can’t explain their answers, and raise real questions about consent and credit for the data they were trained on. People still have to check the work and take responsibility for it.
